india/tamil-nadu/madurai.intro:
Madurai is one of the oldest living cities in India, and it is as famous for its food as for its temple. The city has a culture of late night eating, with stalls and restaurants serving hot parottas and spicy curries long after dark.

This page explains what Madurai is known for, what to eat and where to wander, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose, whether you are on a temple tour or just passing through.

sections.body:
Madurai is known for the Meenakshi Amman temple, with its colorful towers and carved halls, which stands at the center of the old city. The streets around it are laid out in concentric squares, and markets sell flowers, brass, silk and sweets.

The city is called the city that never sleeps, since its temple festivals and night markets keep people out late. It is also famous for jasmine flowers and for a style of cooking that is bold and spicy.

The best known specialty is parotta, a layered flatbread, served with a spicy salna or with egg and meat dishes. Kari dosai, a dosa topped with minced meat, and jigarthanda, a cold drink with milk, almond gum and ice cream, are Madurai originals.

There is also a strong tradition of mutton and chicken curries, banana leaf meals and idlis served with spicy powders. Sweet shops sell halwa and traditional snacks, and filter coffee is a daily habit.

The Meenakshi temple is the main attraction, and the Thirumalai Nayak palace shows a different style of architecture. The Gandhi memorial museum and the Vandiyur tank offer quieter visits.

Nearby, the temples of Alagar Koil and Thiruparankundram are popular, and Kodaikanal hills are within reach for a cooler trip. Evenings are the best time for the temple, when lamps are lit and the city is lively.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Madurai
sections.body:
Use Restroze to compare ratings and review counts, and check the photos for the food and the setting. Check the address, since the old city around the temple can be crowded and traffic slow.

For local food, look for restaurants known for parotta and mutton dishes, and for old tiffin places. Use the phone number to confirm timings, since some close in the afternoon and reopen late.

sections.h2: Practical tips for eating in Madurai
sections.body:
The climate is hot for much of the year, and winters from November to February are the most pleasant. Temple visits require modest dress, and shoes are left outside.

Many food places stay open late, so dinner can be a late evening affair. Ask about spice levels, since Madurai food can be hot, and try jigarthanda as a cooling dessert.

faqs.q: What is Madurai famous for in food?
faqs.a: Madurai is famous for parotta with salna, kari dosai, mutton curries and the cold drink jigarthanda.

faqs.q: What is jigarthanda?
faqs.a: It is a chilled Madurai drink made with milk, almond gum, sugar syrup and ice cream.

faqs.q: Is Madurai good for late night food?
faqs.a: Yes. Many stalls and restaurants stay open late, especially near the old city.

india/kerala.intro:
Kerala has been a spice trading center for centuries, and its food shows it. Coconut, pepper, curry leaves, ginger and cardamom appear in everything from fish curries to sweets. Meals are generous and balanced, and each community, whether Hindu, Muslim or Christian, has its own traditions.

This page gives you a feel for the whole state. Use it to understand what Kerala eats, decide which cities to include in your plans, and then open a city page to compare restaurants by ratings, photos and location before you go.

sections.body:
Kerala is known for its backwaters, beaches, hill stations and tea and spice plantations. It has a long coastline on the Arabian Sea, and its towns are shaped by centuries of trade with Arab, Chinese, Portuguese and European merchants.

The state also has a strong tradition of Ayurveda, temple festivals, classical dance and a high level of literacy. Its landscape is green for much of the year, with rice fields, coconut palms and rivers.

A traditional meal, the sadya, is served on a banana leaf with many vegetable dishes, rice, sambar and payasam, especially at festivals. Appam with stew, puttu with kadala curry and Malabar parotta with beef or chicken curry are everyday favorites.

Seafood is a highlight, with fish curry cooked in clay pots, karimeen pollichathu, and prawn dishes. Malabar biryani is famous in the north. Tea, coffee and tender coconut water are widely served.

Kochi, with its old Fort Kochi area, Chinese fishing nets and spice markets, is a popular starting point. Thiruvananthapuram, the capital, has temples and beaches nearby. Alappuzha and Kumarakom are known for houseboat trips through the backwaters.

Munnar and Wayanad offer tea plantations, forests and cool air, and Kozhikode in the north is known for its food heritage. A well planned trip combines a city, a backwater stay and a hill station.

sections.h2: Practical tips for eating in Kerala
sections.body:

Meals are often served on banana leaves, and eating with the right hand is common. Ask about spice levels and about the catch of the day. Vegetarian meals are easy to find, especially around temples.

india/kerala/kochi.intro:
Kochi is a port city on the Arabian Sea, and its food carries the marks of centuries of trade. Arab, Jewish, Portuguese, Dutch and British influences all left something behind, and the result is a city where you can eat toddy shop curries, Syrian Christian stew and fresh seafood in one day.

This page explains what Kochi is known for, what to eat and where to wander, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Kochi is known as the Queen of the Arabian Sea. Its historic area, Fort Kochi, has colonial buildings, old churches, a synagogue and the famous Chinese fishing nets along the shore. The nearby Mattancherry area has spice warehouses and antique shops.

The city is also the commercial capital of Kerala, with a busy harbor, modern malls and a growing arts scene. Every few years the city hosts a major international art event.

Seafood is the star. Look for fish curry with kokum, fried pomfret, karimeen and crab or prawn roasts. Appam with vegetable or meat stew is a classic breakfast, and puttu with a spicy curry is another favorite.

Toddy shops serve spicy meat and fish dishes with rice, and Malabar biryani and beef fry with parotta are common in local eateries. Sweet banana fritters and halwa are sold in bakeries, and tea and coffee are everywhere.

Fort Kochi is best explored on foot, with St Francis Church, the Dutch cemetery and the Chinese fishing nets. Jew Town in Mattancherry has the old synagogue and antique shops.

Boat rides across the harbor, the Marine Drive promenade and the backwaters nearby add variety. Munnar and Alappuzha are popular trips from the city. Evenings by the water are especially pleasant.

india/kerala/thiruvananthapuram.intro:
Thiruvananthapuram, often called Trivandrum, is the capital of Kerala. It is a green, calm city on a series of low hills, with old palaces, temples and a long coastline close by. The food is traditional and homely, centered on rice, coconut and fresh fish.

This page explains what the city is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you pick a place, whether you are visiting for the day or staying longer.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Padmanabhaswamy temple, one of the most famous in the country, and for its royal heritage, which shows in palaces and museums. It is also the seat of the state government and home to many educational and research institutions.

Nearby beaches, including Kovalam, bring visitors to the coast, and the Ayurveda centers and quiet backwater trips add to its appeal.

Look for a traditional Kerala meal of rice with sambar, avial, thoran and fish curry. Appam with stew, puttu with curry, and Malabar parotta with beef or chicken are everyday favorites. Seafood is fresh along the coast, with fish fry and prawn dishes on many menus.

Payasam, a sweet milk pudding, appears at festivals, and banana chips and jaggery sweets are popular snacks. Tea shops serve strong tea with fried snacks such as banana fritters.

The Padmanabhaswamy temple, the Napier Museum and the Kuthiramalika palace are the best known sights. Kovalam and Varkala beaches are a short drive away, and the Poovar backwaters offer a quiet boat ride.

The Ponmudi hill station and the Neyyar dam are popular day trips. Visitors to the temple must follow strict dress rules, and non Hindus are not allowed inside the main sanctum, so check the rules before going.

Use Restroze to compare ratings and review counts, and check the photos for the food and the setting. Check the address, since the city is spread over hills and traffic can be slow near the center.

For local meals, look for places that serve a banana leaf lunch and fresh fish. For beach areas, expect tourist oriented menus and compare ratings carefully. Use the phone number to confirm opening hours.

The weather is warm and humid throughout the year, with heavy rain from June to September. The best months to visit are November to February.

Many traditional restaurants serve lunch at a fixed time and run out of popular dishes early, so go on time. Ask about the fish of the day, and try tender coconut water on a hot afternoon.

faqs.a: It is known for traditional Kerala meals, fish curry, appam with stew, puttu and payasam.

india/maharashtra/nagpur.intro:
Nagpur sits in the eastern part of Maharashtra, in the Vidarbha region, and its food is among the hottest in the state. Saoji cooking, with its dark, deeply spiced gravies, is the signature style, and the city is also known as the orange city for the fruit grown around it.

This page explains what Nagpur is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Nagpur is known as the geographic center of India and as a major orange growing area. It is also an important center for the Dalit Buddhist community, with the large Deekshabhoomi stupa, and it hosts the winter session of the state legislature.

The city has wide roads, lakes and a relaxed pace, and it serves as a gateway to tiger reserves in central India.

Saoji mutton and chicken are the stars, cooked with a spice mix that gives a deep, fiery gravy. They are eaten with roti or rice. Tarri poha, a breakfast of flattened rice topped with a spicy curry, is a local favorite, and patodi rassa, a gram flour dish, is a well loved vegetarian choice.

Sweet shops sell santra barfi made from oranges, and street stalls serve kachori, samosa and chaat. Tea is available at every corner.

Deekshabhoomi, Futala Lake, Ambazari Lake and the Raman Science Center are popular sights in the city. Sitabuldi Fort and the old markets show the older side of Nagpur.

Tadoba and Pench tiger reserves are within a few hours by road and draw wildlife visitors. Ramtek, a hill temple town, is another easy trip.

india/maharashtra/nashik.intro:
Nashik is a holy city on the Godavari river and the wine capital of India. Pilgrims come for its ancient temples, and visitors come for vineyard tours and tastings in the hills around it. The food is local, robust and spicy.

This page explains what Nashik is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Nashik is one of the four places where the Kumbh Mela festival is held, and its riverfront ghats and temples draw pilgrims throughout the year. The town of Trimbak, with its famous Shiva temple, is close by.

The region is also known for grapes and onions, and a growing number of wineries welcome visitors for tours and tastings.

Nashik is known for its misal pav, a spicy sprouted bean curry topped with farsan and served with bread. Look also for sabudana vada, thalipeeth and traditional Maharashtrian thalis. Chivda, a savory snack mix, is a popular gift to take home.

Street stalls near the old city serve vada pav, bhel and sweet jalebi, and locally grown grapes and fruits are sold in season. Wines from the area are served in restaurants.

Panchavati, with its ghats and temples, and the Kalaram temple are central to the city. Trimbakeshwar, Pandavleni caves and the Anjaneri hill are popular visits nearby.

Vineyard tours are usually done in a half day, and the best season is from November to March, when the grapes are harvested. Sula and other wineries have tasting rooms, but check each place for opening times.

sections.body:

Use the phone number to confirm timings, since some places close in the afternoon.

The weather is pleasant for much of the year, and the monsoon turns the hills green. Pilgrim crowds are heaviest around festivals, so plan ahead. If you plan to taste wine, arrange a driver, and carry water when you walk around the ghats.

Thane sits just north of Mumbai, and it has grown into a city of its own, with lakes, hills and busy shopping streets. Its restaurants serve commuters, families and office crowds, so the choice is broad, from old family eateries to new cafes.

sections.body:
Thane is known as the city of lakes, with many water bodies that give it a calmer feel than Mumbai. It sits at the edge of the Sanjay Gandhi National Park, and the hills on one side offer green views.

The city is also a transport hub, with a major railway station, and a place where many residents travel daily to Mumbai for work.

Thane is known for misal, with local places claiming particular recipes, and for vada pav, pav bhaji and Maharashtrian thalis. Seafood is widely served, with fish curries, fried fish and prawn dishes inspired by the nearby coast.

Chinese street food, biryani and Punjabi dishes are also popular, and many bakeries and sweet shops line the market streets. Tea stalls are busy in the morning and evening.

Upvan Lake, Masunda Lake and the Tikuji Ni Wadi area are popular for evening walks and food. The Yeoor hills offer easy trails inside the national park.

Thane also has old temples and a large creek with birdlife in the colder months. Mumbai is a short train ride away if you want to combine both cities in one trip.

Traffic is heaviest on weekday evenings, so plan a bit earlier or later. The monsoon brings heavy rain, and winter is the most comfortable time for walking by the lakes. Ask about spice levels and about vegetarian options.

Navi Mumbai was planned as a sister city to Mumbai, and it has wide roads, tidy sectors and modern malls. Its restaurants range from old fishing village eateries to new family places, so it is a good city to explore for a relaxed meal.

sections.h2: What Navi Mumbai is known for
sections.body:
Navi Mumbai is known for its planned layout, with neat nodes such as Vashi, Nerul, Belapur and Kharghar. It has a large wholesale market, a long creek with flamingos in season and a growing number of offices and malls.

The city links to Mumbai by bridge, rail and road, and it is close to the Elephanta ferry routes and to the Panvel hills.

Seafood is a highlight, with local Koli and Agri community dishes such as fish curry, fried bombil and prawns. Look for Maharashtrian thalis, misal pav and vada pav at neighborhood eateries. Many restaurants in the market areas serve Chinese and North Indian food.

Fresh seafood is sold in the wholesale markets, and street food stalls near stations serve quick bites. Sweet shops sell traditional sweets and savory snacks.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Navi Mumbai
sections.body:
The Vashi bridge and the harbor area are a good start, and the Nerul and Belapur areas have temples and gardens. The Pandavkada waterfall and the Karnala bird sanctuary are popular day trips.

The flamingos at the creek and wetlands appear in the colder months. Many visitors combine a trip to the city with a trip to Mumbai, which is easily reached by train.

india/maharashtra/aurangabad.intro:
Aurangabad, now also called Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, is a city of history in the Marathwada region. It is the base for the Ajanta and Ellora caves, and its Mughal past shows in old gates, tombs and a rich tradition of meat dishes and sweets.

This page explains what the city is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known as the gateway to the Ajanta and Ellora caves, two of the great rock cut sites of India. The Bibi Ka Maqbara, a tomb often compared to the Taj Mahal, and the fort of Daulatabad lie close by.

It is also known for Himroo and Paithani weaving and for a food culture that blends Mughal and Marathwada traditions.

Look for naan qalia, a rich mutton curry served with naan, and for biryani and kebabs. Many places serve Maharashtrian thalis, jowar bhakri with thecha, and pithla. Tarri poha and misal are common breakfasts.

Sweet shops offer halwa and traditional sweets, and tea shops are busy all day. Many eateries are in the older parts of the city and are known for generations of the same recipes.

The Ajanta caves, with their painted walls, are a day trip, and the Ellora caves, including the Kailasa temple, are closer to the city. Bibi Ka Maqbara, Panchakki and Daulatabad Fort are among the main sights nearby.

Grishneshwar temple near Ellora and the old city gates add to a full visit. The caves are closed one day each week, so check before you plan.

Summers are hot, so the best time to visit is from October to March. The caves involve a lot of walking, so wear comfortable shoes. Carry water, and eat a good meal before a long day of sightseeing.

india/madhya-pradesh.intro:
Madhya Pradesh sits at the heart of India, and its food reflects that position, drawing on the north, the west and the tribal cooking of its forests. Wheat, millet, maize, lentils and plenty of ghee form the base, with sweet and savory snacks that are famous across the country.

This page gives you a feel for the whole state. Use it to understand what each region eats, decide which cities to include in your plans, and then open a city page to compare restaurants by ratings, photos and location.

sections.h2: What Madhya Pradesh is known for
sections.body:
Madhya Pradesh is known as the heart of India. It has the temples of Khajuraho, the Buddhist stupas of Sanchi, the fort at Gwalior and several of the country's best known tiger reserves, including Bandhavgarh and Kanha.

The state also has a deep tradition of handloom weaving in Chanderi and Maheshwar, and a mix of cities with lakes, palaces and old markets.

Poha with jalebi is the famous breakfast, especially in Indore, and the city is known for its late night sarafa market. Dal bafla, a baked wheat ball served with lentils and ghee, is a traditional meal. Bhutte ka kees, made with corn, is a local snack.

Bhopal is known for its Mughlai food, with kebabs, biryani and nihari. Sweet shops offer malpua, mawa bati and the famous chai and savory snacks, and sugarcane juice is sold in summer.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Madhya Pradesh
sections.body:
Bhopal has lakes, museums and old mosques, and Indore is known for its palaces and markets. Ujjain is a holy city with the Mahakaleshwar temple, and Gwalior has a great hill fort.

Khajuraho, Sanchi and the tiger reserves round out a longer trip. Pachmarhi, a hill station, is popular in the warmer months. Distances are large, so plan by region.

india/madhya-pradesh/bhopal.intro:
Bhopal is the capital of Madhya Pradesh and a city of lakes, with an old walled core and a green, spacious new town. Its food has a Mughlai character, a result of centuries of rule by a line of Nawabs, and the old city is full of kebab stalls and bakeries.

This page explains what Bhopal is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Bhopal is known as the city of lakes. The Upper Lake and Lower Lake form the heart of the city, and the old town around them has mosques, palaces and markets. It is also known for its museums and for the nearby Buddhist site of Sanchi.

It blends old and new, with a calm, green modern side and a busy old city.

Bhopal is known for its kebabs, biryani, nihari and paya, served in the old city at stalls and small restaurants. Poha with jalebi is a common breakfast, and bun maska and tea are popular in cafes.

Sweet specialties include the Bhopali paan and mawa sweets, and in winter, stalls sell warm snacks. Fish from the lakes is served in some local restaurants.

The Upper Lake, with boat rides and a promenade, is a pleasant place for the evening. Taj ul Masajid, one of the largest mosques in the country, the Bharat Bhavan arts center and the tribal museum are major sights.

The rock shelters of Bhimbetka and the Buddhist stupas of Sanchi are within easy reach for a day trip. The old city is best explored on foot, early in the day.

india/madhya-pradesh/indore.intro:
Indore is one of the great food cities of India. The city starts its day with poha and jalebi, goes through the day with snacks at every corner and ends with a famous night market where jewelers turn into food stalls after closing.

sections.body:
Indore is known as the commercial capital of Madhya Pradesh and a city with a long history under the Holkar rulers. Its palaces, temples and clean streets are often praised, and it is a hub for trade, education and food.

Food is the city's pride. Locals speak of favorite shops that have served the same recipes for generations.

Poha topped with sev and served with jalebi is the iconic breakfast. Try garadu, a fried yam, bhutte ka kees, sabudana khichdi, dahi vada and the many snacks of the Sarafa night market. Dal bafla is the traditional main meal.

Sweet shops serve rabri, malpua and shikanji, a spiced lemon drink. Namkeen, the savory snack mixes made in the city, are famous and are often taken home as gifts.

Rajwada, the old palace of the Holkars, and Lal Baag Palace are among the major sights, and the Kanch Mandir, a glass temple, is unusual. The Chhatri Bagh shows royal memorials.

Day trips include Ujjain, with the Mahakaleshwar temple, and Mandu, a ruined hilltop city, and Maheshwar on the Narmada river for weavers and temples.

india/punjab.intro:
Punjab is the land of wheat fields and generous kitchens. Its food is hearty, rich in dairy and cooked over wood and clay ovens, and it has shaped what many people around the world think of as Indian food.

This page gives you a feel for the whole state. Use it to understand what Punjab eats, decide which cities to include in your plans, and then open a city page to compare restaurants by ratings, photos and location.

sections.body:
Punjab is known as the breadbasket of India, with fields of wheat and rice and a farming culture that has a strong sense of hospitality. The state is the spiritual home of Sikhism, and its best known sight is the Golden Temple in Amritsar.

It is also known for its music, its festivals such as Baisakhi and Lohri, and its lively dhabas along the main roads.

Think of butter chicken, dal makhani, sarson ka saag with makki di roti, stuffed parathas, chole kulche and tandoori dishes. Lassi is served thick in tall glasses, often topped with cream. Kheer, jalebi and phirni are favorite sweets.

Amritsari fish and kulcha are well known, and roadside dhabas serve food with plenty of butter and ghee. Langar, the free community meal at gurdwaras, is a simple vegetarian meal open to everyone.

Amritsar has the Golden Temple, the Jallianwala Bagh memorial and the Wagah border ceremony. Ludhiana is an industrial city with a famous agricultural university, and Patiala and Anandpur Sahib add history and festivals.

Chandigarh, close by, is a planned city with gardens and museums. The winter months are best for a trip.

india/punjab/amritsar.intro:
Amritsar is a city where food and faith go together. Around the Golden Temple, the streets are full of stalls and old shops that have been serving kulcha, lassi and sweets for generations, and the temple itself serves thousands of free meals a day.

This page explains what Amritsar is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Amritsar is known for the Golden Temple, the holiest shrine of Sikhism, and for its close link to history, from the Jallianwala Bagh memorial to the border ceremony at Wagah. The old walled city is a maze of lanes and markets.

The city is also known for its food, with a reputation that draws visitors from across the country.

The famous dish is Amritsari kulcha, a stuffed bread baked in a clay oven and served with chole and a cube of butter. Amritsari fish, fried in a spiced gram flour batter, and chicken tikka are other staples. Lassi, thick and sweet, is served in tall glasses.

For sweets, try jalebi, phirni and the milk based desserts of the old city. Tea is served strong and milky. At the Golden Temple, the langar serves a simple vegetarian meal to all.

The Golden Temple is open day and night and is especially beautiful in the early morning and at night. Jallianwala Bagh and the partition museum are nearby. The Wagah border ceremony in the late afternoon is a popular excursion.

The Durgiana temple and the old bazaars add to a full day. Dress modestly, cover your head and remove your shoes at religious sites.

sections.body:
Ludhiana is known as the Manchester of India for its hosiery and woolen industry, and for the Punjab Agricultural University, which helped lead the green revolution. It is a busy, prosperous city with markets and malls.

Its food culture is generous. Meals are big, and hospitality is a point of pride.

Expect butter chicken, tandoori dishes, dal makhani, paneer dishes and stuffed parathas with butter and curd. Sarson ka saag with makki di roti is a winter favorite, and chole bhature, kulcha and lassi are served at many local places.

Sweet shops offer jalebi, gulab jamun and kheer, and street stalls serve chaat and golgappa. Along the highways, large dhabas are famous for their dishes cooked over open fires.

The Punjab Agricultural University museum, the Lodhi fort, and Rakh Bagh park are among the places to visit. The city's markets are known for woolens and textiles.

Nearby, Sikh historic sites and the Sutlej river are good day trips, and Chandigarh and Amritsar are easy to reach by road or rail.

sections.body:
Gurugram is known as a business and technology hub, home to many corporate offices. It grew rapidly from a small town into a city of glass towers, golf courses and large shopping centers.

The old city still has temples and markets, and nearby villages offer a glimpse of rural Haryana. Dining is a major leisure activity, especially on weekends.

Gurugram has a wide mix of cuisines, from North Indian and Chinese to Italian, Japanese and Middle Eastern. Local Haryanvi food, with milk, butter, bajra rotis and dishes such as kadhi, is available at some restaurants and roadside places.

Cafes, bakeries and brunch spots are popular, as are sports bars and rooftop restaurants. Street stalls near markets serve chaat, momos and rolls.

Cyber Hub is the most famous dining and nightlife area, and the malls along MG Road are busy shopping and entertainment centers. Kingdom of Dreams, a theater and food complex, and the Sultanpur bird sanctuary are nearby attractions.

The Aravalli biodiversity park and the old Sheetla Mata temple add quieter visits. Delhi is a short drive away for a longer trip.
